description: Shared ZeroAlloc Renovate defaults. Extend from a repo with:
"extends": ["config:recommended", "github>ZeroAlloc-Net/.github"]
and drop that repo's own "schedule" — this replaces it.
Updates flow continuously, but nothing is raised until a release has been out
for three days. That is the point at which a bad or yanked release has usually
been found, so it buys the same protection a weekly batch window did without
the batching: an update published on Tuesday arrives Friday rather than
waiting for the following Monday.
Security fixes opt out of both the wait and any schedule. minimumReleaseAge is
set back to null under vulnerabilityAlerts, because otherwise the three-day
wait would inherit and delay exactly the updates that must not wait.
schedule: [] means 'any time', so a security PR is still raised immediately
even in a repo that keeps a schedule of its own. Without it, a repo scheduled
'before 6am on monday' parks security fixes under Awaiting Schedule until the
next window — which is how ZeroAlloc.Serialisation sat with a high-severity
MessagePack advisory while audit-as-error made main unbuildable, unnoticed
because CI only runs on push and pull_request.
semanticCommitType fix, rather than Renovate's default chore: release-please
treats chore as non-releasable, so a security fix would merge to main and
never ship — the package consumers restore would stay vulnerable. fix cuts a
patch release.
internalChecksFilter is left at its default of strict, so updates still inside
the three-day wait are held back rather than raised and then blocked.
vulnerabilityAlerts carries no prPriority: Renovate only accepts prPriority
inside packageRules, and renovate-config-validator rejects it here. It was
silently ignored rather than prioritising anything. Security PRs already skip
the three-day wait and any schedule, which is what actually gets them out
quickly; prPriority would only have reordered a queue held back by prConcurrentLimit.
packageRules group each ZeroAlloc family into one PR, keyed on the publishing
repo. Most repos — ZeroAlloc.Mediator and ZeroAlloc.ORM among them — release
with a single-component manifest, so everything they publish shares one version
and ships together. Some, such as ZeroAlloc.Saga, are multi-component and version
their packages independently; grouping still holds there, because a group PR
carries whatever updates exist regardless of their versions.
What makes grouping necessary rather than merely tidy is that several of these
packages cannot be upgraded apart. A source generator bumped without its runtime
emits code the older
runtime cannot satisfy: ZeroAlloc.Saga#92 took ZeroAlloc.Mediator.Generator to
v5 on its own and failed with CS0051, while the sibling PR carrying only
ZeroAlloc.Mediator went green. Neither half could merge alone, and no amount
of retrying either PR would have fixed it.
separateMajorMinor is off for these groups. Grouping alone is not enough: a
family whose runtime offers a minor and whose generator offers a major would
still be split back into two PRs by the default major/minor separation, which
is the exact failure this is meant to prevent.
Groups are keyed on the publishing repo rather than the package prefix, which
is why ZeroAlloc.TypeConversions sits in the ORM group — it ships from
ZeroAlloc.ORM at ORM's version, so it moves when ORM moves.
A new ZeroAlloc repo with no rule here keeps today's behaviour of one PR per
package. That is safe for a family with no generator; add a rule when the
repo starts publishing one.
First-party packages skip the three-day wait.
minimumReleaseAge exists so that a bad or yanked release surfaces before it
reaches us. That reasoning is about releases we do not control. These come
from repositories in this org and from MarcelRoozekrans' own account, so they
have already been through our CI and review; the wait adds latency without
adding information.
It also works against us. Several of these families must move together — a
source generator bumped without its runtime emits code the older runtime
cannot satisfy — and a cross-repo fix is only really shipped once every
consumer has taken it. Three days per hop makes a chain of first-party
packages take over a week to settle.
ZeroAlloc packages are owned on nuget.org by ZeroAlloc.NET; AI.Sentinel,
AdoNet.Async, MemoryLens and RoslynCodeLens by MarcelRoozekrans. A bare
ZeroAlloc package id also exists, hence ($|\.) rather than a trailing dot.
Everything not matched here keeps the three-day wait.
ASP.NET Core and EF Core ship one package major per .NET major, and that
major is the ONLY framework it supports: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore
10.0.10 and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web 10.0.10 each carry a single
lib/net10.0. A repo that still targets net8.0 or net9.0 therefore cannot take
them, and the restore fails with NU1202 before anything compiles.
Projects here express that by referencing the same package once per target
framework behind a Condition — ZeroAlloc.Scheduling.Dashboard.Blazor pins
8.0.2*, 9.0.1* and 10.0.1* for net8.0, net9.0 and net10.0 respectively.
Renovate does not read the Condition attribute, so it sees three references
to one package and offers to move all three to the newest major. The net10.0
one is already correct; the other two become unrestorable.
For these packages the major is a TARGET FRAMEWORK decision, not a dependency
one: it changes only when a net11.0 target is added along with its own
conditional reference. So no major is ever raised automatically, while minor
and patch updates keep flowing in every stream — including 10.x, so net10.0
targets still receive EF Core and ASP.NET Core updates.
This replaces an earlier pair of rules that capped 8.x below 9 and 9.x below
10. Those left 10.x uncapped, so the identical breakage would have returned
when .NET 11 shipped. Blocking the major outright needs no new rule per
release.
Deliberately NOT applied to Microsoft.Extensions.*: those are multi-targeted.
Microsoft.Extensions.Http 10.0.10 ships net462, netstandard2.0, net8.0, net9.0
and net10.0, so constraining it would block upgrades that restore perfectly.
Leave global.json alone. With rollForward set, the sdk version field is a
FLOOR, not a target: the newest installed SDK is selected regardless. Renovate
raising it to the latest patch therefore buys nothing and breaks any runner
whose image has not caught up yet, because rollForward only ever rolls
forward, never back to an older SDK.
That is not hypothetical. A publish failed on a runner whose newest SDK was
10.0.400 against a floor of 10.0.401, leaving a tagged release with no package
on nuget.org and needing a manual rescue. Other repos with the identical pin
succeeded in the same window, which is the signature of a race against the
runner-image rollout rather than a deterministic break.
ZeroAlloc.Templates#372 lowered the floor back to the GA band, and Renovate
raised it straight back to 10.0.401 in #384 a few hours later. Fixing the
value without disabling the manager just loses the fix at the next SDK patch.
Raise the floor by hand when a repo genuinely needs a newer SDK feature.
